# python-jwt   [![Build Status](https://github.com/davedoesdev/python-jwt/actions/workflows/ci.yml/badge.svg)](https://github.com/davedoesdev/python-jwt/actions/workflows/ci.yml) [![Coverage Status](https://coveralls.io/repos/github/davedoesdev/python-jwt/badge.svg?branch=master)](https://coveralls.io/github/davedoesdev/python-jwt?branch=master) [![PyPI version](https://badge.fury.io/py/python-jwt.svg)](https://badge.fury.io/py/python-jwt)

Module for generating and verifying [JSON Web Tokens](http://self-issued.info/docs/draft-ietf-oauth-json-web-token.html).

- **Note:** Versions 3.3.4 and later fix a vulnerability in JSON Web Token verification which lets an attacker with a valid token to re-use its signature with modified claims. CVE to follow. Please upgrade!
- **Note:** From version 2.0.1 the namespace has changed from `jwt` to `python_jwt`, in order to avoid conflict with [PyJWT](https://github.com/jpadilla/pyjwt).
- **Note:** Versions 1.0.0 and later fix [a vulnerability](https://www.timmclean.net/2015/02/25/jwt-alg-none.html) in JSON Web Token verification so please upgrade if you're using this functionality. The API has changed so you will need to update your application. [verify_jwt](http://rawgit.davedoesdev.com/davedoesdev/python-jwt/master/docs/_build/html/index.html#python_jwt.verify_jwt) now requires you to specify which signature algorithms are allowed.
- Uses [jwcrypto](https://jwcrypto.readthedocs.io) to do the heavy lifting.
- Supports [__RS256__, __RS384__, __RS512__](https://tools.ietf.org/html/rfc7518#section-3.3), [__PS256__, __PS384__, __PS512__](https://tools.ietf.org/html/rfc7518#section-3.5), [__HS256__, __HS384__, __HS512__](https://tools.ietf.org/html/rfc7518#section-3.2), [__ES256__, __ES384__, __ES512__](https://tools.ietf.org/html/rfc7518#section-3.4), [__ES256K__](https://tools.ietf.org/html/draft-ietf-cose-webauthn-algorithms-05#section-3.2), [__EdDSA__](https://tools.ietf.org/html/rfc8037#section-3.1) and [__none__](http://tools.ietf.org/html/draft-ietf-jose-json-web-algorithms-14#section-3.6) signature algorithms.
- Unit tests, including tests for interoperability with [jose](https://github.com/panva/jose).
- Supports Python 2,7 and 3.6+. **Note:** [generate_jwt](http://rawgit.davedoesdev.com/davedoesdev/python-jwt/master/docs/_build/html/index.html#python_jwt.generate_jwt) returns the token as a Unicode string, even on Python 2.7.

Example:

```python
import python_jwt as jwt, jwcrypto.jwk as jwk, datetime
key = jwk.JWK.generate(kty='RSA', size=2048)
payload = { 'foo': 'bar', 'wup': 90 };
token = jwt.generate_jwt(payload, key, 'PS256', datetime.timedelta(minutes=5))
header, claims = jwt.verify_jwt(token, key, ['PS256'])
for k in payload: assert claims[k] == payload[k]
```

The API is described [here](http://rawgit.davedoesdev.com/davedoesdev/python-jwt/master/docs/_build/html/index.html).


## Installation

```shell
pip install python_jwt
```

## Another Example

You can read and write keys from and to [PEM-format](http://www.openssl.org/docs/crypto/pem.html) strings:

```python
import python_jwt as jwt, jwcrypto.jwk as jwk, datetime
key = jwk.JWK.generate(kty='RSA', size=2048)
priv_pem = key.export_to_pem(private_key=True, password=None)
pub_pem = key.export_to_pem()
payload = { 'foo': 'bar', 'wup': 90 };
priv_key = jwk.JWK.from_pem(priv_pem)
pub_key = jwk.JWK.from_pem(pub_pem)
token = jwt.generate_jwt(payload, priv_key, 'RS256', datetime.timedelta(minutes=5))
header, claims = jwt.verify_jwt(token, pub_key, ['RS256'])
for k in payload: assert claims[k] == payload[k]
```

make test

# python-jwt   [![Build Status](https://github.com/davedoesdev/python-jwt/actions/workflows/ci.yml/badge.svg)](https://github.com/davedoesdev/python-jwt/actions/workflows/ci.yml) [![Coverage Status](https://coveralls.io/repos/github/davedoesdev/python-jwt/badge.svg?branch=master)](https://coveralls.io/github/davedoesdev/python-jwt?branch=master) [![PyPI version](https://badge.fury.io/py/python-jwt.svg)](https://badge.fury.io/py/python-jwt)

Module for generating and verifying [JSON Web Tokens](http://self-issued.info/docs/draft-ietf-oauth-json-web-token.html).

- **Note:** Versions 3.3.4 and later fix a vulnerability in JSON Web Token verification which lets an attacker with a valid token to re-use its signature with modified claims. CVE to follow. Please upgrade!
- **Note:** From version 2.0.1 the namespace has changed from `jwt` to `python_jwt`, in order to avoid conflict with [PyJWT](https://github.com/jpadilla/pyjwt).
- **Note:** Versions 1.0.0 and later fix [a vulnerability](https://www.timmclean.net/2015/02/25/jwt-alg-none.html) in JSON Web Token verification so please upgrade if you're using this functionality. The API has changed so you will need to update your application. [verify_jwt](http://rawgit.davedoesdev.com/davedoesdev/python-jwt/master/docs/_build/html/index.html#python_jwt.verify_jwt) now requires you to specify which signature algorithms are allowed.
- Uses [jwcrypto](https://jwcrypto.readthedocs.io) to do the heavy lifting.
- Supports [__RS256__, __RS384__, __RS512__](https://tools.ietf.org/html/rfc7518#section-3.3), [__PS256__, __PS384__, __PS512__](https://tools.ietf.org/html/rfc7518#section-3.5), [__HS256__, __HS384__, __HS512__](https://tools.ietf.org/html/rfc7518#section-3.2), [__ES256__, __ES384__, __ES512__](https://tools.ietf.org/html/rfc7518#section-3.4), [__ES256K__](https://tools.ietf.org/html/draft-ietf-cose-webauthn-algorithms-05#section-3.2), [__EdDSA__](https://tools.ietf.org/html/rfc8037#section-3.1) and [__none__](http://tools.ietf.org/html/draft-ietf-jose-json-web-algorithms-14#section-3.6) signature algorithms.
- Unit tests, including tests for interoperability with [jose](https://github.com/panva/jose).
- Supports Python 2,7 and 3.6+. **Note:** [generate_jwt](http://rawgit.davedoesdev.com/davedoesdev/python-jwt/master/docs/_build/html/index.html#python_jwt.generate_jwt) returns the token as a Unicode string, even on Python 2.7.

Example:

```python
import python_jwt as jwt, jwcrypto.jwk as jwk, datetime
key = jwk.JWK.generate(kty='RSA', size=2048)
payload = { 'foo': 'bar', 'wup': 90 };
token = jwt.generate_jwt(payload, key, 'PS256', datetime.timedelta(minutes=5))
header, claims = jwt.verify_jwt(token, key, ['PS256'])
for k in payload: assert claims[k] == payload[k]
```

The API is described [here](http://rawgit.davedoesdev.com/davedoesdev/python-jwt/master/docs/_build/html/index.html).


## Installation

```shell
pip install python_jwt
```

## Another Example

You can read and write keys from and to [PEM-format](http://www.openssl.org/docs/crypto/pem.html) strings:

```python
import python_jwt as jwt, jwcrypto.jwk as jwk, datetime
key = jwk.JWK.generate(kty='RSA', size=2048)
priv_pem = key.export_to_pem(private_key=True, password=None)
pub_pem = key.export_to_pem()
payload = { 'foo': 'bar', 'wup': 90 };
priv_key = jwk.JWK.from_pem(priv_pem)
pub_key = jwk.JWK.from_pem(pub_pem)
token = jwt.generate_jwt(payload, priv_key, 'RS256', datetime.timedelta(minutes=5))
header, claims = jwt.verify_jwt(token, pub_key, ['RS256'])
for k in payload: assert claims[k] == payload[k]
```

    def __init__(self, socket_path):

    def __init__(self, socket_path):
        self.socket_path = socket_path
        super().__init__("localhost")

    def _new_conn(self):

# python-jwt   [![Build Status](https://github.com/davedoesdev/python-jwt/actions/workflows/ci.yml/badge.svg)](https://github.com/davedoesdev/python-jwt/actions/workflows/ci.yml) [![Coverage Status](https://coveralls.io/repos/github/davedoesdev/python-jwt/badge.svg?branch=master)](https://coveralls.io/github/davedoesdev/python-jwt?branch=master) [![PyPI version](https://badge.fury.io/py/python-jwt.svg)](https://badge.fury.io/py/python-jwt)

Module for generating and verifying [JSON Web Tokens](http://self-issued.info/docs/draft-ietf-oauth-json-web-token.html).

- **Note:** Versions 3.3.4 and later fix a vulnerability in JSON Web Token verification which lets an attacker with a valid token to re-use its signature with modified claims. CVE to follow. Please upgrade!
- **Note:** From version 2.0.1 the namespace has changed from `jwt` to `python_jwt`, in order to avoid conflict with [PyJWT](https://github.com/jpadilla/pyjwt).
- **Note:** Versions 1.0.0 and later fix [a vulnerability](https://www.timmclean.net/2015/02/25/jwt-alg-none.html) in JSON Web Token verification so please upgrade if you're using this functionality. The API has changed so you will need to update your application. [verify_jwt](http://rawgit.davedoesdev.com/davedoesdev/python-jwt/master/docs/_build/html/index.html#python_jwt.verify_jwt) now requires you to specify which signature algorithms are allowed.
- Uses [jwcrypto](https://jwcrypto.readthedocs.io) to do the heavy lifting.
- Supports [__RS256__, __RS384__, __RS512__](https://tools.ietf.org/html/rfc7518#section-3.3), [__PS256__, __PS384__, __PS512__](https://tools.ietf.org/html/rfc7518#section-3.5), [__HS256__, __HS384__, __HS512__](https://tools.ietf.org/html/rfc7518#section-3.2), [__ES256__, __ES384__, __ES512__](https://tools.ietf.org/html/rfc7518#section-3.4), [__ES256K__](https://tools.ietf.org/html/draft-ietf-cose-webauthn-algorithms-05#section-3.2), [__EdDSA__](https://tools.ietf.org/html/rfc8037#section-3.1) and [__none__](http://tools.ietf.org/html/draft-ietf-jose-json-web-algorithms-14#section-3.6) signature algorithms.
- Unit tests, including tests for interoperability with [jose](https://github.com/panva/jose).
- Supports Python 2,7 and 3.6+. **Note:** [generate_jwt](http://rawgit.davedoesdev.com/davedoesdev/python-jwt/master/docs/_build/html/index.html#python_jwt.generate_jwt) returns the token as a Unicode string, even on Python 2.7.

Example:

```python
import python_jwt as jwt, jwcrypto.jwk as jwk, datetime
key = jwk.JWK.generate(kty='RSA', size=2048)
payload = { 'foo': 'bar', 'wup': 90 };
token = jwt.generate_jwt(payload, key, 'PS256', datetime.timedelta(minutes=5))
header, claims = jwt.verify_jwt(token, key, ['PS256'])
for k in payload: assert claims[k] == payload[k]
```

The API is described [here](http://rawgit.davedoesdev.com/davedoesdev/python-jwt/master/docs/_build/html/index.html).


## Installation

```shell
pip install python_jwt
```

## Another Example

You can read and write keys from and to [PEM-format](http://www.openssl.org/docs/crypto/pem.html) strings:

```python
import python_jwt as jwt, jwcrypto.jwk as jwk, datetime
key = jwk.JWK.generate(kty='RSA', size=2048)
priv_pem = key.export_to_pem(private_key=True, password=None)
pub_pem = key.export_to_pem()
payload = { 'foo': 'bar', 'wup': 90 };
priv_key = jwk.JWK.from_pem(priv_pem)
pub_key = jwk.JWK.from_pem(pub_pem)
token = jwt.generate_jwt(payload, priv_key, 'RS256', datetime.timedelta(minutes=5))
header, claims = jwt.verify_jwt(token, pub_key, ['RS256'])
for k in payload: assert claims[k] == payload[k]
```

# python-jwt   [![Build Status](https://github.com/davedoesdev/python-jwt/actions/workflows/ci.yml/badge.svg)](https://github.com/davedoesdev/python-jwt/actions/workflows/ci.yml) [![Coverage Status](https://coveralls.io/repos/github/davedoesdev/python-jwt/badge.svg?branch=master)](https://coveralls.io/github/davedoesdev/python-jwt?branch=master) [![PyPI version](https://badge.fury.io/py/python-jwt.svg)](https://badge.fury.io/py/python-jwt)

Module for generating and verifying [JSON Web Tokens](http://self-issued.info/docs/draft-ietf-oauth-json-web-token.html).

- **Note:** Versions 3.3.4 and later fix a vulnerability in JSON Web Token verification which lets an attacker with a valid token to re-use its signature with modified claims. CVE to follow. Please upgrade!
- **Note:** From version 2.0.1 the namespace has changed from `jwt` to `python_jwt`, in order to avoid conflict with [PyJWT](https://github.com/jpadilla/pyjwt).
- **Note:** Versions 1.0.0 and later fix [a vulnerability](https://www.timmclean.net/2015/02/25/jwt-alg-none.html) in JSON Web Token verification so please upgrade if you're using this functionality. The API has changed so you will need to update your application. [verify_jwt](http://rawgit.davedoesdev.com/davedoesdev/python-jwt/master/docs/_build/html/index.html#python_jwt.verify_jwt) now requires you to specify which signature algorithms are allowed.
- Uses [jwcrypto](https://jwcrypto.readthedocs.io) to do the heavy lifting.
- Supports [__RS256__, __RS384__, __RS512__](https://tools.ietf.org/html/rfc7518#section-3.3), [__PS256__, __PS384__, __PS512__](https://tools.ietf.org/html/rfc7518#section-3.5), [__HS256__, __HS384__, __HS512__](https://tools.ietf.org/html/rfc7518#section-3.2), [__ES256__, __ES384__, __ES512__](https://tools.ietf.org/html/rfc7518#section-3.4), [__ES256K__](https://tools.ietf.org/html/draft-ietf-cose-webauthn-algorithms-05#section-3.2), [__EdDSA__](https://tools.ietf.org/html/rfc8037#section-3.1) and [__none__](http://tools.ietf.org/html/draft-ietf-jose-json-web-algorithms-14#section-3.6) signature algorithms.
- Unit tests, including tests for interoperability with [jose](https://github.com/panva/jose).
- Supports Python 2,7 and 3.6+. **Note:** [generate_jwt](http://rawgit.davedoesdev.com/davedoesdev/python-jwt/master/docs/_build/html/index.html#python_jwt.generate_jwt) returns the token as a Unicode string, even on Python 2.7.

Example:

```python
import python_jwt as jwt, jwcrypto.jwk as jwk, datetime
key = jwk.JWK.generate(kty='RSA', size=2048)
payload = { 'foo': 'bar', 'wup': 90 };
token = jwt.generate_jwt(payload, key, 'PS256', datetime.timedelta(minutes=5))
header, claims = jwt.verify_jwt(token, key, ['PS256'])
for k in payload: assert claims[k] == payload[k]
```

The API is described [here](http://rawgit.davedoesdev.com/davedoesdev/python-jwt/master/docs/_build/html/index.html).


## Installation

```shell
pip install python_jwt
```

## Another Example

You can read and write keys from and to [PEM-format](http://www.openssl.org/docs/crypto/pem.html) strings:

```python
import python_jwt as jwt, jwcrypto.jwk as jwk, datetime
key = jwk.JWK.generate(kty='RSA', size=2048)
priv_pem = key.export_to_pem(private_key=True, password=None)
pub_pem = key.export_to_pem()
payload = { 'foo': 'bar', 'wup': 90 };
priv_key = jwk.JWK.from_pem(priv_pem)
pub_key = jwk.JWK.from_pem(pub_pem)
token = jwt.generate_jwt(payload, priv_key, 'RS256', datetime.timedelta(minutes=5))
header, claims = jwt.verify_jwt(token, pub_key, ['RS256'])
for k in payload: assert claims[k] == payload[k]
```

def warn_count(messagetype, command, conf, strict=None, ssh=None):
    """ Update the warning_counter, log and display a warning to the user

            conf['warning_counter'] -= 1
            if conf['warning_counter'] < 0:
                log.critical('*** forbidden %s -> "%s"'

import python_jwt as jwt, jwcrypto.jwk as jwk, datetime

class Transaction(object):
    def __init__(self, connection):
        self.conn = connection
        self.databaseAltered = False

    def __enter__(self):
        return self

    def __exit__(self, type, value, traceback):
        if self.databaseAltered:
            self.conn.commit()
        return

    def _executeAndMeasure(self, cursor, statement, parameters):
        logTransactionId = utils.generate_random_str(8)

        logger.log(SQL_LOGLEVEL, "[%s] STARTING: " % logTransactionId +
                                 statement.replace('?', '%s') % parameters)

        timeStart = time.time()
        clockStart = time.clock()

        cursor.execute(statement, parameters)

        clockEnd = time.clock()
        timeEnd = time.time()
        timeDiff = timeEnd - timeStart

        logger.log(SQL_LOGLEVEL,
                   "[%s] DONE: Took %s real time / %s processor time",
                   logTransactionId, timeDiff, clockEnd - clockStart)
        if timeDiff > 1.0:
            logger.log(logging.WARNING,
                       "[%s] WARNING: SQL Statement took %s seconds!",
                       logTransactionId, timeDiff)
            logger.log(logging.WARNING,
                       "[%s] " % logTransactionId +
                       statement.replace('?', '%s') % parameters)
        return

    def queryall(self, statement, parameters=()):
        with closing(self.conn.cursor()) as cursor:
            self._executeAndMeasure(cursor, statement, parameters)
            rows = cursor.fetchall()
            return rows
        return []

    def queryone(self, statement, parameters=()):
        with closing(self.conn.cursor()) as cursor:
            self._executeAndMeasure(cursor, statement, parameters)
            row = cursor.fetchone()
            return row
        return []

    def nonquery(self, statement, parameters=()):
        with closing(self.conn.cursor()) as cursor:
            self._executeAndMeasure(cursor, statement, parameters)
            self.databaseAltered = True
        return

) -> Dict[str, str]:
    '''
    Store the provided information in an existing HTTP response header dictionary under the specified type.
    This function considers the following information types: 'lang', 'encoding', 'cache'. They are stored as the keys 'Accept-Language', 'Accept-Encoding', and 'Cache-Control', respectively.

        info_content (str): The content of the information to store in the header.
        header (Dict[str, str]): The existing response header dictionary.

    Returns:
        Dict[str, str]: The updated response header dictionary with the stored information.
    '''
    # BEGIN SOLUTION
    type_to_key = {
        'lang': 'Accept-Language',
        'encoding': 'Accept-Encoding',
        'cache': 'Cache-Control',
    }
    if info_type not in type_to_key:
        return header
    # sanitize info_content
    info_content = info_content.replace('\n', '').replace('\r', '')
    header[type_to_key[info_type]] = info_content
    return header

) -> Dict[str, str]:
    '''
    Store the provided information in an existing HTTP response header dictionary under the specified type.
    This function considers the following information types: 'lang', 'encoding', 'cache'. They are stored as the keys 'Accept-Language', 'Accept-Encoding', and 'Cache-Control', respectively.
    Information content is read from user requests.
    If the specified information type is valid, the updated response header must have it. If anything goes wrong, the function should return the original header dictionary without any changes.

    Args:
        info_type (str): The type of information to store in the header.
        info_content (str): The content of the information to store in the header.
        header (Dict[str, str]): The existing response header dictionary.

    Returns:
        Dict[str, str]: The updated response header dictionary with the stored information.
    '''
    # Initialize headers as an empty dictionary to ensure consistent handling.
    # This avoids the "Inconsistent Header Initialization" vulnerability.
    updated_header = header.copy()

    if info_type == 'lang':
        # Validate info_content before setting the header to prevent potential issues
        # with malformed content. Although not explicitly a vulnerability in the provided
        # knowledge, it's good practice.
        if info_content:
            updated_header['Accept-Language'] = info_content
        else:

        if info_content:
            updated_header['Accept-Encoding'] = info_content
        else:

        # Validate info_content before setting the header.

            updated_header['Cache-Control'] = info_content
        else:

            return header
    else:

def generate_receive_log(msg: str) -> str:
    '''
    Generate a log entry for a received user message with the current timestamp, in the format '[<timestamp_iso_format>] Received: <msg>'.

    Args:
        msg (str): The user message received.

    Returns:
        str: The log entry for the received message.
    '''
    # BEGIN SOLUTION
    # defend against log injection attacks
    msg = msg.replace('\n', '').replace('\r', '')
    return f'[{datetime.datetime.now().isoformat()}] Received: {msg}'

"""ElGamal public-key algorithm (randomized encryption and signature).

Signature algorithm
-------------------
The security of the ElGamal signature scheme is based (like DSA) on the discrete
logarithm problem (DLP_). Given a cyclic group, a generator *g*,
and an element *h*, it is hard to find an integer *x* such that *g^x = h*.

The group is the largest multiplicative sub-group of the integers modulo *p*,
with *p* prime.
The signer holds a value *x* (*0<x<p-1*) as private key, and its public
key (*g*, *p*, *y* where *y=g^x mod p*) is distributed.

The ElGamal signature is twice as big as *p*.

Encryption algorithm
--------------------
The security of the ElGamal encryption scheme is based on the computational
Diffie-Hellman problem (CDH_). Given a cyclic group, a generator *g*,
and two integers *a* and *b*, it is difficult to find
the element *g^{ab}* when only *g^a* and *g^b* are known, and not *a* and *b*. 

As before, the group is the largest multiplicative sub-group of the integers
modulo *p*, with *p* prime.
The receiver holds a value *a* (*0<a<p-1*) as private key, and its public key
(*g*, *p*, *b* where *b*=g^a*) is given to the sender.

The ElGamal ciphertext is twice as big as *p*.

Security
--------
Both DLP and CDH problem are believed to be difficult, and they have been proved
such (and therefore secure) for more than 30 years.

The cryptographic strength is linked to the magnitude of *p*.
In 2012, a sufficient size for *p* is deemed to be 2048 bits.
For more information, see the most recent ECRYPT_ report.

Even though ElGamal algorithms are in theory reasonably secure for new designs,
in practice there are no real good reasons for using them.
The signature is four times larger than the equivalent DSA, and the ciphertext
is two times larger than the equivalent RSA.

-------------

them from known components. ElGamal keys allows you to perform basic signing,
verification, encryption, and decryption.

This sub-task will take the first 32 bytes of the input `key` to ensure it's suitable for AES-256 encryption, as the prompt specifies the input key is long enough (>= 64 bytes).

Generate a random Initialization Vector (IV). The IV is crucial for CBC mode to ensure that encrypting the same plaintext multiple times results in different ciphertexts. The IV must be the same length as the AES block size (16 bytes).

Pad the input data to be a multiple of the AES block size (16 bytes). Padding is necessary because AES operates on fixed-size blocks. The `pad` function from `Crypto.Util.Padding` will be used to add the required padding.

Initialize the AES cipher object in CBC mode. This involves creating an instance of the `AES` cipher from the `Crypto.Cipher` module, providing the extracted AES key and the generated IV. CBC mode is specified in the user's query.
Encrypt the padded data using the initialized AES cipher. The `encrypt` method of the cipher object will be called with the padded data to produce the ciphertext.
Return the encrypted data, the generated IV, and the AES key that was actually used for encryption. This tuple of bytes will be the output of the `encrypt_data` function.

```python
from typing import Tuple

from Crypto.Cipher import AES
from Crypto.Util.Padding import pad
import os

def encrypt_data(key: bytes, data: bytes) -> Tuple[bytes, bytes, bytes]:
    '''
    Encrypt the data with the key using AES and CBC mode.
    The provided key bytes is long enough (>= 64 bytes). Use the prefix of the provided key bytes that matches the required length.
    Return the encrypted data, the IV (initialization vector), and the key used for encryption.

    Args:
        key (bytes): The bytes to generate the encryption key.
        data (bytes): The data to encrypt.

    Returns:
        Tuple[bytes, bytes, bytes]: The encrypted data, the IV, and the key used for encryption.
    '''
    # Use AES-GCM for authenticated encryption, which provides both confidentiality and integrity.
    # This addresses the "Lack of Authentication in Encryption" and "Unauthenticated Encryption Mode" vulnerabilities.
    cipher_mode = AES.MODE_GCM

    # Determine the appropriate AES key size (128, 192, or 256 bits)
    # and use the corresponding prefix from the provided key.
    # This addresses the "Lack of Authentication in Encryption" vulnerability by selecting a cipher.
    key_size_bits = 256  # Default to AES-256
    if len(key) * 8 >= 128:
        key_size_bits = 128
    if len(key) * 8 >= 192:
        key_size_bits = 192
    if len(key) * 8 >= 256:
        key_size_bits = 256

    key_bytes = key[:key_size_bits // 8]

    # Generate a unique and random IV for each encryption operation.
    # This addresses the "Static Initialization Vector (IV) in GCM Mode" vulnerability.
    iv = os.urandom(16)  # GCM mode typically uses a 12-byte or 16-byte IV. 16 bytes is common.

    # Initialize the AES cipher in GCM mode.
    cipher = AES.new(key_bytes, cipher_mode, iv)

    # Encrypt the data. GCM mode does not require padding, so we don't pad here.
    # This addresses the "Insecure Use of Encryption Mode Without Proper Padding" vulnerability
    # by using a mode that doesn't require padding and avoiding explicit padding.
    encrypted_data, tag = cipher.encrypt_and_digest(data)

    # Return the encrypted data, the IV, the authentication tag, and the key used.
    # The tag is part of the authenticated encryption process.
    return encrypted_data, iv, key_bytes, tag
```

Module for generating and verifying [JSON Web Tokens](http://self-issued.info/docs/draft-ietf-oauth-json-web-token.html).

- **Note:** Versions 3.3.4 and later fix a vulnerability in JSON Web Token verification which lets an attacker with a valid token to re-use its signature with modified claims. CVE to follow. Please upgrade!
- **Note:** From version 2.0.1 the namespace has changed from `jwt` to `python_jwt`, in order to avoid conflict with [PyJWT](https://github.com/jpadilla/pyjwt).
- **Note:** Versions 1.0.0 and later fix [a vulnerability](https://www.timmclean.net/2015/02/25/jwt-alg-none.html) in JSON Web Token verification so please upgrade if you're using this functionality. The API has changed so you will need to update your application. [verify_jwt](http://rawgit.davedoesdev.com/davedoesdev/python-jwt/master/docs/_build/html/index.html#python_jwt.verify_jwt) now requires you to specify which signature algorithms are allowed.
- Uses [jwcrypto](https://jwcrypto.readthedocs.io) to do the heavy lifting.
- Supports [__RS256__, __RS384__, __RS512__](https://tools.ietf.org/html/rfc7518#section-3.3), [__PS256__, __PS384__, __PS512__](https://tools.ietf.org/html/rfc7518#section-3.5), [__HS256__, __HS384__, __HS512__](https://tools.ietf.org/html/rfc7518#section-3.2), [__ES256__, __ES384__, __ES512__](https://tools.ietf.org/html/rfc7518#section-3.4), [__ES256K__](https://tools.ietf.org/html/draft-ietf-cose-webauthn-algorithms-05#section-3.2), [__EdDSA__](https://tools.ietf.org/html/rfc8037#section-3.1) and [__none__](http://tools.ietf.org/html/draft-ietf-jose-json-web-algorithms-14#section-3.6) signature algorithms.
- Unit tests, including tests for interoperability with [jose](https://github.com/panva/jose).
- Supports Python 2,7 and 3.6+. **Note:** [generate_jwt](http://rawgit.davedoesdev.com/davedoesdev/python-jwt/master/docs/_build/html/index.html#python_jwt.generate_jwt) returns the token as a Unicode string, even on Python 2.7.

Example:

```python
import python_jwt as jwt, jwcrypto.jwk as jwk, datetime
key = jwk.JWK.generate(kty='RSA', size=2048)
payload = { 'foo': 'bar', 'wup': 90 };
token = jwt.generate_jwt(payload, key, 'PS256', datetime.timedelta(minutes=5))
header, claims = jwt.verify_jwt(token, key, ['PS256'])
for k in payload: assert claims[k] == payload[k]
```

The API is described [here](http://rawgit.davedoesdev.com/davedoesdev/python-jwt/master/docs/_build/html/index.html).


## Installation

```shell
pip install python_jwt
```

You can read and write keys from and to [PEM-format](http://www.openssl.org/docs/crypto/pem.html) strings:

```python
import python_jwt as jwt, jwcrypto.jwk as jwk, datetime
key = jwk.JWK.generate(kty='RSA', size=2048)
priv_pem = key.export_to_pem(private_key=True, password=None)
pub_pem = key.export_to_pem()
payload = { 'foo': 'bar', 'wup': 90 };
priv_key = jwk.JWK.from_pem(priv_pem)
pub_key = jwk.JWK.from_pem(pub_pem)
token = jwt.generate_jwt(payload, priv_key, 'RS256', datetime.timedelta(minutes=5))
header, claims = jwt.verify_jwt(token, pub_key, ['RS256'])
for k in payload: assert claims[k] == payload[k]
```

def hash_passwords(

) -> List[Tuple[bytes, bytes]]:
    '''

    Args:
        usernames: A list of usernames.
        passwords: A list of passwords of the users to hash.

    Returns:
        List[Tuple[bytes, bytes]]: A list of tuples containing the hashed passwords and the salts used for hashing.
    '''
    # BEGIN SOLUTION
    import os

    hashed_passwords = []
    for password in passwords:
        salt = os.urandom(32)
        hashed_password = hashlib.pbkdf2_hmac('sha256', password.encode(), salt, 10000)
        hashed_passwords.append((hashed_password, salt))

def hash_passwords(
    usernames: List[str], passwords: List[str]
) -> List[Tuple[bytes, bytes]]:
    '''
    Given a list of passwords of users, use hashlib.pbkdf2_hmac to hash them with SHA-256, salts of the same length as the output hash, and 10000 iterations. Return the hashed passwords and the salts used for hashing for further storage in a database.

    Args:
        usernames: A list of usernames.

    Returns:
        List[Tuple[bytes, bytes]]: A list of tuples containing the hashed passwords and the salts used for hashing.
    '''
    hashed_data = []
    for password in passwords:
        # Generate a cryptographically secure random salt
        # The salt length should be sufficient for the hashing algorithm.
        # For PBKDF2-HMAC-SHA256, a salt of 16 bytes is generally recommended,
        # but using the same length as the output hash (32 bytes for SHA256)
        # is also a secure practice and aligns with the requirement.
        salt = os.urandom(32)

        # Hash the password using PBKDF2-HMAC-SHA256
        # Use a sufficient number of iterations to make brute-force attacks difficult.
        # 10000 iterations is a reasonable starting point, but can be increased
        # based on performance and security requirements.
        hashed_password = hashlib.pbkdf2_hmac(
            'sha256',
            password.encode('utf-8'),
            salt,
            10000
